subtitle: Ordering politely, paying, and what is on the menu
words.intro: Café Riquet in Leipzig has served coffee since 1908, under two bronze elephants. The words of a café afternoon: what you order, what you say, what you pay.

reading.intro: Maya is in Leipzig for the day. In the oldest café in town she meets the one thing nobody warned her about: the cake counter.
reading.photos[0].caption: Quiche im Café Riquet. Das Café hat auch Frühstück bis 14 Uhr.
reading.photos[1].caption: Die Fassade: zwei Elefanten aus Bronze. Riquet hat früher Tee und Schokolade aus Asien importiert.
reading.en: Waiter: Hello. Is this seat free? Yes? Here you are. What would you like? · Maya: A coffee, please. With milk, no sugar. · Waiter: A Milchkaffee. And something to eat? The cakes are at the front, at the counter. · Maya: I see them. Twelve cakes. I have a problem. · Waiter: Everyone has that problem. My tip: the cheesecake. Or the chocolate cake. Or both. · Maya: A slice of cheesecake, please. And a glass of water. · Waiter: Certainly. The water costs nothing, this is Leipzig. · Twenty minutes later. · Maya: The bill, please! · Waiter: One Milchkaffee, three fifty. One slice of cheesecake, three fifty. That comes to seven euros. · Maya: Eight, please. Keep the change. · Waiter: Thank you! And? The cake? · Maya: Very good. I'll come back tomorrow. For the chocolate cake.
reading.fact: In Germany you say the total you want to pay, tip included: *Acht, bitte* on a bill of seven. Five to ten per cent is normal. Leaving coins on the table is not done.

grammar[0].blocks[0].note: No verb needed: the thing, bitte.
grammar[0].blocks[1].title: What the waiter says, and what you answer
grammar[0].blocks[1].note: einen Kaffee, einen Tee (der-words after möchten take -en); eine Limonade; ein Wasser, ein Stück.
grammar[0].blocks[2].text: Germans split the bill by what each person had. The waiter asks *together or separately?* and expects *getrennt* at a table of friends. Nobody is being mean.
grammar[0].check.title: Mini-Check
grammar[0].fact: The *Kaffeehaus* is Vienna's gift to the German-speaking world: one coffee buys you the table for the afternoon, the newspapers on their wooden holders, and nobody asks you to leave.
grammar[1].subheading: The three verbs that carry a café conversation
grammar[1].photo.caption: Zupfkuchen und Kaffee. Ich habe Hunger, ich möchte Kuchen, ich bin glücklich.
grammar[1].blocks[0].title: sein and haben
grammar[1].blocks[0].note: sein has no pattern at all. haben is regular, except that du *hast* and er *hat* lose the b. möchte (would like) is the polite way to order or ask — and ich and er share one form.
grammar[1].blocks[1].blocks[0].text: German *has* hunger: Ich habe **Hunger** (I’m hungry), **Durst** (thirsty), **Angst** (afraid), **Zeit** (I have time). But your age is sein: Ich *bin* zwanzig.
grammar[1].blocks[1].blocks[1].title: wir and sie are twins
grammar[1].blocks[1].blocks[1].text: In both verbs, *wir* and *sie · Sie* have the same form: wir sind, sie sind; wir haben, sie haben. Learn four forms, get six.
grammar[1].check.title: Mini-Check
grammar[1].fact: *Ich bin satt* is “I'm full”. *Ich bin voll* means you are drunk. Both will happen in a German café, so learn the difference early.

document.intro: A real menu. Find the drinks and their prices; the bottom tells you how the cake works.
document.fact: *Kaffee Crema* is a long black coffee, the German default. Espresso comes with a glass of water on request, and *auf Wunsch* means exactly that: if you wish.
